slides.text:
**Git 3.0 is swapping its default hash from SHA-1 to SHA-256.**

Scott Chacon, GitHub's co-founder, says it will break tooling for years.

For a threat that barely applies to real attacks.

**SHA-1 counts as "broken" on paper.**

Nobody has used that break on a real project.
bullets: SHAttered (2017) and Shambles (2020) proved the collision.
Cost: tens of thousands of dollars in GPU time.
Cheaper still: about $40k to just buy a maintainer's trust.

slides.text:
Chacon's real point: **trust was never about the hash.**

It comes from where you pull your code.

An idea he traces back to Linus Torvalds.

Not everyone agreed.

One developer said SHAttered was never theoretical.

panel.small: when SHAttered proved it as a working exploit

slides.text:
The migration cost is real, too.

**One developer's CI broke outright on SHA-256.**
bullets: GitHub still has no public SHA-256 support.
Submodules mixing both hashes have no clean fix.
That developer rebuilt their repos under SHA-1.

slides.text:
Others pushed back on "train wreck."

SHA-1 repos keep working, untouched.

**One developer called it a friendly migration.**

**My rule: map the real attack path first.**

One commenter guessed the real driver is compliance.

panel.small: bans SHA-1 outright at some firms

slides.text:
Have you shipped a security fix that broke more than it saved?

**Tell me what happened,** and save this for your next CI migration.
